Q is a theory result equating quantum local differential privacy with the quantum statistical query model, deriving strong data processing inequalities for relative entropy under restricted measurements, whereas P is an engineering framework for pipeline integrity using hash-chained audit trails and observable-deviation subtype contracts; the only shared surface is that both reason about limited-measurement access to quantum states and both mention cloud QPU settings. Q provides differential-privacy amplification bounds for quantum data encodings and quantum-inspired sampling, while P is a variational-accuracy metric (V-score) and dataset for many-body ground-state benchmarking; there is no shared technical object, since P's energy-variance metric involves no user dataset, no privacy threat model and no sampling-based privacy budget. Q tailors surface codes to known non-uniform and correlated single- and two-qubit noise via Clifford conjugation with a matching decoder, whereas P is a vendor press release reporting a Quantum Volume figure on a trapped-ion system; QV is a heuristic holistic benchmark with no encoding, syndrome extraction or decoder to which Q's tailoring could attach, so the only link is the generic notion of device-specific noise asymmetry. Both concern training parameterised quantum circuits, and Q's variance bounds on gradients and QFIM-rank controllability arguments could in principle inform QAOA angle-setting, but Q's results are specific to Hamming-weight preserving ansätze on fixed-weight subspaces, whereas P's QAOA ansatz is a cost-plus-mixer circuit that does not preserve Hamming weight, so the trainability theorems do not transfer to P's circuits. Both concern incoherent noise on near-term processors, and there is a concrete hook in that Q's subgroup-symmetrisation gadget suppresses both coherent and stochastic errors by 1/M, which speaks directly to P's error-per-cycle control parameter driving the XEB phase transition: running the weak-link RCS circuit with M redundant copies and subgroup projection would shift the transition point and test whether purification can push a noisy circuit back into the computationally complex phase. However, RCS fidelity depends on error rates accumulated across all 67 qubits and 32 cycles, and Q's M-fold copy overhead plus O(p^{-1}) sampling cost is prohibitive at that scale, so the composition is analytically suggestive rather than experimentally runnable as stated. Interest sits above generic because the pairing names a sharp quantity in P's statistical model (error per cycle versus coherent evolution) that Q's gadget directly rescales, but it stops short of top marks since purification is a broadly applicable error-suppression wrapper for any noisy sampling workload.

Q's subgroup-stabilisation purification is a generic error-suppression gadget requiring M redundant copies plus ancilla-controlled permutation circuits, and P is a NISQ-oriented Trotter-compression scheme whose whole point is to fit shallow dynamics circuits within limited hardware fidelity, so the composition is conceivable — purified copies of the compressed time-evolved state could sharpen the rate-coefficient observables P extracts — but nothing in P's protocol specifically needs subspace projection rather than any other mitigation, and the copy overhead directly contradicts P's stated aim of minimising qubit and gate resources. The hook is thus at the level of 'error suppression applied to a noisy simulation workload', which is the universal-adapter pattern: Q's gadget attaches equally well to any near-term dynamics demonstration. Interest is further capped because P's compression already trades accuracy against fidelity in a tunable way, making the interaction between variational compression error (coherent, systematic, not suppressed by copy-projection in the manner Q analyses) and Q's 1/M suppression suggestive but not concretely developed by either text.

Q offers a verification-derived benchmarking protocol that yields formal statements about device quality under a consistency assumption, but it is framed around circuit-model computations, whereas P is an analog neutral-atom reservoir whose learning performance is the figure of merit; no concrete hook transfers, since Q's protocol neither certifies P's analog Hamiltonian dynamics nor stresses P's kernel-geometry advantage claim, which rests on classical-versus-quantum kernel separation rather than on device fidelity. Q surveys analogue quantum programming tools (including annealing) and rates their readiness for HPC integration, while P is a hybrid graph-contraction plus D-Wave annealing solver for TSP; the overlap is real in that P's classical contraction plus annealer pipeline is precisely the sort of hybrid HPC-QPU workflow Q's readiness taxonomy classifies, but Q supplies no technique that P's workload consumes and P's results do not test any of Q's claims. Q is a QAOA-based attack on the Shortest Vector Problem, using pretrained fixed angles and a zero-vector-avoiding Hamiltonian encoding to extrapolate heuristic time complexity; P is a 120-qubit digital Trotter simulation of Fermi-Hubbard dynamics with error suppression and TDVP benchmarking. P's quantum samples could feed Q's warm-start annealing stage, and Q's approximation-ratio/Hamming-distance scaling methodology is a direct test of P's claim that the quantum solver is competitive with Gurobi but short of SA and Burer-Monteiro. Interest is high but not maximal because the graph classes differ (unit-disk MIS versus 3-regular MaxCut) and warm-starting a classical heuristic with quantum samples is a fairly generic move within this family, so the composition needs work to be device-specific.

Q is a sample-complexity result on estimating Tsallis relative entropy and Hellinger-distance state certification for low-rank states, whereas P is a hardware demonstration of the Parity Architecture compiling a 50-qubit QFT with process fidelity around 10^-2; the only contact point is the generic notion of comparing states, and P's fidelity is already characterised by process tomography/benchmarking rather than by tolerant certification of an unknown low-rank state. Both concern quantum simulation of correlated many-body systems, but the technical content barely touches: Q benchmarks adiabatic-inspired variational ground-state preparation for a small molecule (BeH2, ansatz/schedule choices, LBFGS), while P measures dynamical structure factors of a spin chain by Trotterised real-time evolution on 50 superconducting qubits and compares to neutron-scattering data. Interest is low because 'use a better ground-state preparation routine' attaches to any simulation demo of this family and does not exploit anything specific to either paper.

A curator might sketch a mapping of G-AQC-PQC ansätze onto the three-rail 18-qubit array, but nothing in either text makes that pairing specific or experimentally sharp.

Both papers address the sampling-overhead economics of unbiased error suppression: Q builds a shot-budget-aware benchmarking framework that quantifies confidence that an estimated energy falls within classical bounds under probabilistic error cancellation overhead, while P measures exactly that exponential sample cost for error detection on up to 74 physical qubits and estimates pseudothresholds. Interest is high but not maximal because Q's framework is somewhat of a general shot-accounting wrapper that could attach to any QEM method's overhead model, and P's memory and logical-computation benchmarks are not optimization workloads such as the Fermi-Hubbard instance Q studies.

Q's randomisation and symmetrisation methods target exactly the failure modes P's workflow depends on: P draws large numbers of samples from 77-qubit, 10,570-gate Heron circuits and feeds them into sample-based diagonalisation, so measurement-error mitigation sample complexity and noise-estimation-circuit mitigation are concrete hooks, and Q's parallelisation-based symmetrisation could be inserted into P's readout and mitigation stages on the same superconducting hardware. The predictability-of-noisy-circuit-performance result is also pertinent to P's reliance on configuration recovery from biased samples.

Q tailors surface codes to non-uniform single- and two-qubit noise via Clifford conjugation with a matching decoder, while P runs a fragment-based SQD electronic-structure workflow on near-term hardware with no error-correction layer at all — SQD relies on post-selection and classical diagonalisation of sampled configurations, not on encoded logical qubits, so Q's construction does not attach to P's circuits without a wholesale change of regime. Both sides sit in state verification on hardware, and there is a real hook: Q's verification technique needs only remote preparation of X-Y plane single-qubit states, which is precisely the resource GHZ-type entangled resources plus Pauli-basis measurements on Quantinuum's trapped-ion device could supply, and P already layers error detection onto its GHZ runs, so Q's error-detection-style trap verification could in principle replace or complement the compressed-sensing fidelity estimate. Interest is capped at the middling level because Q's verification is a generic wrapper applicable to essentially any X-Y-plane preparation demo, the universal-adapter pattern, rather than something specific to compressed sensing of GHZ fidelity.

Interest sits above generic error mitigation because purifying a genuinely mixed non-equilibrium steady state is a sharper question than purifying a pure target, but the gadget still attaches to most noisy-state preparations, keeping it near the universal-adapter pattern.

Q analyses non-Markovian dephasing and depolarising dynamics of GHZ and W states, whereas P benchmarks LR-QAOA circuits on a 98-qubit trapped-ion QPU against exascale statevector simulation; the only shared element is the generic notion that noise degrades quantum outputs, with no concrete hook since P's noise-tolerance boundary is determined statistically from sampling distributions rather than from entanglement decay of cat or W states, and Q offers no diagnostic or protocol P could adopt. Q's saturation and revival results concern fixed few-parameter noise channels on symmetric states, which neither predict nor stress P's empirical 93-qubit coherence threshold on deep two-qubit-gate circuits. Any integration story would amount to vaguely suggesting that non-Markovian memory might explain Helios-1's performance, a generic appeal that would attach to any noisy-hardware benchmark paper.

Q is a qLDPC memory construction (radial codes from lifted products, single-shot decoding, circuit-level noise simulation), while P is a NISQ-level empirical study of noise-induced landscape flattening for p=1 QAOA on ibm_fez with ZNE; the only link is the generic observation that both concern quantum error, so corr stays low. There is no concrete hook: radial codes require long-range connectivity and many physical qubits per logical qubit and would not be applied to a 156-qubit variational QUBO run, and P's LSC metric says nothing that stresses Q's threshold or overhead claims. Any 'encode QAOA in radial codes' story is speculative, hardware-infeasible on Heron r2, and of the universal-adapter kind (any code plus any variational demo), so int is minimal.

Q is a symbolic-execution verifier for fault-tolerance of QECC gadgets, while P is an unencoded random circuit sampling experiment whose entire point is noise-driven phase transitions in XEB fidelity with no encoded logical operations, stabiliser gadgets, or error-correction circuitry for the tool to consume. Q studies how non-Markovian dephasing and depolarising noise degrades or partially preserves multipartite GHZ and W entanglement, whereas P inserts Cayley-parameterised unitary adapters into frozen LLM projection layers and runs them on a 156-qubit IBM device; the only shared element is that noise on superconducting hardware matters, which is not a concrete technical hook. P's adapter circuits are not multipartite entanglement-distribution protocols and its reported 'noise-expressivity phase transition' concerns trainability of variational blocks, not entanglement saturation under information back-flow, so Q's saturation values neither transfer to nor stress P's perplexity claims. Any story about characterising the QPU's non-Markovianity to explain P's noise transition is generic device-noise commentary of the universal-adapter kind, so interest stays low.

Q's accreditation protocol is built precisely for analogue simulators without two-qubit gates and with non-identical error maps across runs, and P's workload is a real-time Hamiltonian-evolution experiment on a 12-qubit XXZ chain whose output is a weighted sum of expectation values at shifted pump amplitudes — a family of related evolutions that is exactly the repeated-simulation structure Q's traps are designed to bound, so the technical hook (Q certifies the estimates P reports as noise-resilient but unverified) is concrete rather than generic. Interest is high because accrediting each parameter-shift term would turn P's higher-order response functions into bounded-error certified quantities, and because P's spin-chain dynamics is a candidate instance for Q's simulation-based advantage route; it falls slightly short of 1 since Q's protocol is a verification wrapper that could in principle attach to many analogue simulation demonstrations, giving it some universal-adapter flavour.

Q provides an accreditation protocol for analogue Hamiltonian simulators that explicitly removes two-qubit gates and universal Hamiltonians, whereas P is a gate-model measurement technique on IBM superconducting processors using Grover-type amplification and shallow oracle-free circuits — the platform and primitive assumptions are disjoint, so Q's trap-based accreditation cannot wrap P's circuits. The only tenuous overlap is that both estimate observables (P's infinite-temperature correlator resembles quantities an analogue simulator might probe), but Q's guarantees do not transfer to sampled trace-like estimators with engineered ensembles, and P's amplitude amplification does not help Q's noise-robustness claims. Any integration story would amount to a generic 'verify the estimator' pitch that attaches to any observable-estimation paper, so interest is low.

Q gives quantum query algorithms and lower bounds for graph distance parameters (eccentricity, radius, diameter) in the adjacency-list oracle model, whereas P encodes graphs into a tunable Rydberg Hamiltonian to build a kernel for graph classification; the only shared element is that the input objects are graphs, with no oracle, no distance metric, and no complexity claim in P that Q's bounds could stress. One could imagine adding diameter or eccentricity as an extra graph descriptor to P's feature vector, but that is a classical preprocessing step on graphs of 2-32 nodes where Q's asymptotic speedups and Ω(√(nm)) bounds are irrelevant, so nothing composes on the same hardware. Interest is low because the pairing yields no runnable experiment and no reinterpretation of either result.

Q optimises an adiabatic schedule for Grover-style unstructured search under bounded coherence, whereas P scores hardware on Hamiltonian-simulation tasks (condensed matter, NMR, chemistry ground states, classical optimisation) via a distinguishability-cost metric; the only overlap is that both involve time-dependent Hamiltonian evolution, and P's optimisation benchmark concerns annealing-style objective encodings rather than oracle-based search, so no specific technique transfers. Q's schedule is not a valid task in P's five settings and P's metric certifies incorrect outputs rather than measuring premature-termination success probability, giving no concrete hook. Any integration story (add unstructured search as a sixth benchmark) is generic boilerplate that would attach to any algorithm paper, so interest is low.

Q delegates and verifies variational quantum algorithms via blind measurement-based verification, while P is a quantum lattice Boltzmann algorithm for incompressible CFD with walls, inlets and forcing — a non-variational, block-encoding/linear-algebraic pipeline, so Q's per-optimisation-step trap-based verification has no concrete hook into P's circuit. The only link is the generic 'cloud CFD user might want secure delegation' story, which is the universal-adapter pattern: Q's protocol attaches to any delegated quantum workload and would apply identically to any vendor demo. Neither does P need the secrecy guarantee (its inputs are published benchmark flows such as Taylor-Green and lid-driven cavity) nor does Q's simulation of the Transverse Field Ising Model stress P's complexity-scaling claims.

Q applies a BERT language model to decode superdense-coding messages over noisy quantum channels, whereas P is a contract-based integrity-verification framework for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines using observable-deviation tests and hash-chained audit logs; the only overlap is the generic notion of noisy quantum stages, with no shared circuit, protocol or metric. One could imagine P auditing Q's ML-assisted decoder as an unverified pipeline stage, but P's observable-deviation contract is defined over channel diamond-norm deviations of computational stages, not over a classical post-processing model trained on measurement strings, so the hook is speculative rather than concrete. Interest is low because any such story is the universal-adapter kind — P's verifier attaches to essentially any quantum stage — and nothing about superdense coding specifically stresses or extends P's Z-only-sneaky override analysis.

Q supplies hardware-tailored logical Clifford compilation for stabiliser codes, while P's QSP circuits for linear PDEs are unencoded NISQ demonstrations dominated by QFT and phase-rotation subroutines, i.e. non-Clifford resources that Q's framework does not address; the only hook is the generic wish to run P's deep circuits fault-tolerantly, which Q cannot deliver without magic-state or synthesis machinery outside its scope. Consequently corr stays low (broad shared interest in circuit compilation only) and int lower still, since the resulting dossier would be an unspecific 'encode the PDE algorithm one day' note.

Both papers concern characterising deviations of real quantum dynamics from an ideal model, but Q's certification framework assumes black-box access to e^{-iHt} for a time-independent Hamiltonian and tests closeness to a target in Frobenius, Pauli and Schatten p-norms, whereas P's object of study is non-Markovian, correlated pure dephasing from a structured environment across repeated runs of a fixed gate-based circuit — a channel-level, memory-dependent effect that Q's Hamiltonian-distance formalism does not capture. One could imagine using Q's ancilla-free certification to check whether the qubit-plus-environment dynamics in P's NV-centre or IBM setting is close to an assumed joint Hamiltonian, which is why corr is above the different-topics floor, but this requires controllable evolution access P never claims and does not test P's specific quantum-versus-Kraus discrimination claim. Interest is low because the hook reduces to the generic 'certify the device Hamiltonian' adapter that would attach to almost any hardware-noise study rather than to P's particular two-run correlation signature.

Q is a foundational result in equational semantics and synthesis for orthogonal matrices over Z[1/sqrt2], giving a complete axiomatisation of a reversible language extended by Hadamard; P is an empirical shot-count/resilience/cost benchmarking study of VQE for H2 on IBM devices. The only contact point is that both concern quantum circuits: P's tapered hardware-efficient ansatz uses parameterised rotations outside Q's Z[1/sqrt2] fragment, so Q's synthesis algorithm cannot compile or optimise P's circuits, and P's accuracy-versus-cost claims are untouched by an equational completeness theorem. No concrete use, need, stress or composition hook exists, so a curator would find no dossier worth opening beyond the generic 'formal methods meet hardware demo' framing.

Both papers concern the resource cost of fault-tolerant computation, and there is a partial hook: P's model prices the QEM sampling multiplier for NISQ and magic-state/code-distance overhead for FTQC, while Q certifies whether logical error rates are low enough for error mitigation to be efficient and twirls non-transversal logical gates beyond the T gate — a certification-derived input to exactly those cost terms. The hook stays soft, however, because P is a first-order accounting model rather than a circuit or protocol that could be modified to run accreditation, and Q's overhead (extra trap runs) would simply add a term to any energy model, which is close to the universal-adapter pattern. Interest sits below the midpoint: a curator could develop 'energy cost of certified logical computation' and the crossover point Q identifies maps onto P's NISQ/FTQC energy crossover, but neither side needs the other to make its claim.

Q is a ZX-calculus formalisation (the KNOT calculus and its (0,pi)-fragment) of defect braiding in surface codes, whereas P is an analogue neutral-atom graph kernel using Ising-Hamiltonian time evolution and measurement sampling; there is no fault-tolerant circuit in P for KNOT diagrams to describe, and the (0,pi)-fragment cannot express P's continuous-time, non-Clifford dynamics. The only link is the generic aspiration that P's kernel might one day run on encoded qubits, which is neither concrete nor specific to defect braiding. No experiment or composition follows, so interest is minimal.

Q's VBOE protocol builds on measurement-based/gate-model blind delegation with trap-based verification of expectation values, whereas P is an empirical study of forward and reverse annealing schedules on a D-Wave 2000Q analogue annealer; no blind-verification machinery in Q applies to annealing hardware, and P's controls do not supply anything Q needs, so the only shared ground is the generic notion of trusting a cloud QPU's output. One could note that P's portfolio-optimisation instances are delegated to a third-party annealer with no correctness guarantee, but P checks results against known ground truth and reports success probabilities, so verification adds nothing concrete here. The integration story is the universal-adapter kind (verify any delegated quantum computation) and is furthermore blocked by the platform mismatch, capping interest well below 0.5.

Both concern learning with quantum circuits, but the technical objects barely touch: Q analyses Fourier/correlator decompositions of Born-rule sampling distributions in QCBMs and the parameter discrepancy between classical surrogate training and quantum deployment, whereas P proves and demonstrates sample-complexity separations for learning from two-copy entangled measurements on physical states, not for generative sampling models. The nearest hook is that P's shadow-tomography-style baselines and Q's Pauli-propagation/tensor-network surrogates both concern classical simulability of Pauli-observable estimates, so Q's closed-form propagation results could in principle bound the classical side of P's learning tasks, but Q's dequantisation conditions are tied to variational Born-machine ansaetze (IQP, matchcircuits, spin chains) and do not stress P's information-theoretic separation, which holds regardless of surrogate trainability. The integration story is therefore generic — apply a classical-surrogate analysis to a quantum-advantage claim — and would not survive a domain expert's scrutiny, since P's advantage is in experiment count rather than in output-distribution complexity.

Q benchmarks adiabatically-inspired VQE variants whose inner loop evaluates energy expectation values, so P's bounded ZNE could in principle mitigate those estimates, and the physicality bound is arguably meaningful for variational energies subject to a lower bound; however Q's contribution is algorithmic and reported on ideal/simulated landscapes with no noise-mitigation component, and P's benchmark is GHZ/W-state and synthetic circuits, so no concrete hook is asserted on either side. The integration story is the universal-adapter kind — bounded extrapolation attaches to any expectation-value workload — and is weakened further because Q's key difficulties (barren plateaux, zero-gradient regions, non-convex landscapes) are not noise-bias problems that ZNE addresses, though a curator might note that constraining estimates below the variational bound is a slightly less generic pairing than arbitrary observables.

Both concern extracting usable results from noisy NISQ output distributions, but Q's framework is built around energy estimation for optimisation (Fermi-Hubbard), confidence intervals against classical bounds, and PEC sampling overhead, none of which map onto order finding, where the output is a discrete denominator recovered by continued fractions and verified deterministically by modular arithmetic — no bias-corrected expectation value is involved. The only hook is generic: both quantify shot budget versus success probability, and one could in principle recast Q's finite-shot confidence machinery as a shot-budget criterion for recoverability, but Q's entropy-benchmarking and QEM-overhead accounting do not transfer to a problem with a free classical verifier that makes error mitigation largely redundant. Interest is low because the pairing would require rebuilding Q's framework around a different figure of merit rather than composing the two as given.

Q is a classical dequantisation result for variational quantum machine learning models with Hamiltonian data encoding, bounding the frequencies needed to fit a VQC's Fourier series with random Fourier features; P is a hardware framework for n-th order nonlinear spectroscopy that reformulates multi-time response functions as weighted sums of expectation values at finite pump amplitudes via a generalised parameter shift rule. The only shared object is the appearance of finite Fourier/frequency structure and parameter-shift-style sums, but P is a simulation of physical response functions on a 12-qubit XXZ chain with no learning model, no data encoding and no claimed machine-learning advantage, so Q's sampling bounds neither transfer to nor stress P's claims. A curator could at best speculate that Q's spectral sampling might sparsify P's frequency-domain reconstruction, which is generic and unsupported by either text, leaving no specific dossier to open.

Q is a multi-client blind delegated computation protocol demonstrated on a photonic linear Qline network, whereas P is a full-system energy accounting model instantiated on superconducting Heisenberg simulation and VQE workloads with QEM sampling and code-distance overheads; the only shared ground is delegated/cloud quantum computing as a setting, with no technique that transfers or composes. One could in principle ask what the classical communication and per-client rotation overhead of blind computation costs energetically, but P's model is built around QEM sampling multipliers and magic-state factories on gate-based hardware and contains nothing addressing photonic MBQC or communication rounds, so the hook is speculative rather than concrete. The pairing is also a universal-adapter case — an energy model can be pointed at any protocol — so curator interest stays low.

Q is a survey and readiness rating of analogue quantum programming tools (annealing, Hamiltonian simulation) for HPC integration, whereas P concerns classical Bayesian optimisation of variational parameters for a gate-based QAOA workload; the only hook is that QAOA parameter search is a hybrid classical-quantum loop of the kind an HPC-integrated toolchain would host, and Q explicitly scopes itself outside circuit-based integration. No concrete technical transfer exists: Q provides no software artefact that P's optimiser could use, and P's Bayesian surrogate does not stress or compose with any specific analogue tool Q rates. Any integration story (host P's outer loop in an HPC-coupled stack, or map QAOA onto an annealer) is generic and would attach equally to any variational algorithm paper, so interest stays low.

Both papers pursue qubit-frugal encodings of classical combinatorial problems — CGQeMCMC coarse-grains an Ising sampler onto sqrt(n) qubits, PCE compresses m QUBO variables onto O(m^(1/k)) qubits — but the technical hooks do not meet: CGQeMCMC's quantum step is a Hamiltonian-evolution proposal inside a Metropolis chain requiring an explicit spin-block Hamiltonian, whereas PCE's contribution is a variational correlator training loss plus the PAGD classical decoder for dense feasibility constraints, and neither supplies what the other needs. One could imagine using CGQeMCMC as a sampler over the mRNA QUBO, but the dense pairing constraints (~193,000) that motivate PAGD are exactly what a coarse-grained Ising-style proposal handles badly, so the composition is generic 'another QUBO solver' rather than specific. Interest is accordingly low: the pairing is a family-level resemblance in qubit compression, not a specific experiment that would change how either paper is read.

Q certifies an unknown Hamiltonian against a target given access to its time evolution, whereas P is an energy-to-solution study of a variational fine-tuning pipeline on a trapped-ion QPU; P runs shallow parameterised gate circuits and reports no Hamiltonian dynamics or analogue evolution that Q's protocol could take as input. The only hook is the loose shared setting of near-term trapped-ion hardware plus Q's ancilla-free variant being resource-light, which is a generic device-characterisation adapter rather than something that touches P's classification accuracy or its 34-qubit ETS break-even claim. An energy cost per certification experiment could in principle be measured with P's power instrumentation, but that applies to any quantum protocol and so gives no pairing-specific dossier.

Q's robust verification protocol is built on measurement-based trap runs tolerating up to 12.5–25% test failure without fault tolerance, whereas P is a toric-code memory experiment on neutral atoms with mid-circuit loss detection and qubit reloading; the only real hook is the shared concern of distinguishing noise from adversarial deviation, and P's atom-loss detection could in principle supply the erasure information Q's trap-based confidence amplification exploits, but nothing in P's syndrome-extraction workload instantiates a blind delegated computation with classical inputs and outputs. Interest is limited because Q's scheme is a universal-adapter-style security wrapper that attaches to essentially any remotely accessed device, and P demonstrates no delegation, client, or privacy setting for it to bite on; conversely Q explicitly disclaims needing the full fault tolerance P is building toward, so neither side stresses the other's claims.

Q is a multi-client blind delegated computation protocol built on a photonic linear Qline with measurement-based computation, whereas P computes continuous-time quantum-walk centrality on protein residue networks with a small proof-of-principle run on IBM superconducting hardware; there is no shared platform, no MBQC formulation of the walk, and no privacy requirement identified in P. The only hook is the generic observation that any delegated computation could in principle be blinded, which is the universal-adapter pattern and additionally fails here because Q's protocol is tied to a photonic linear network rather than the gate-based Hamiltonian simulation P performs. Protein structures are public PDB entries, so even the privacy motivation that would make a federated-blinded-walk dossier interesting is absent.

Q is a code-capacity-level QEC construction (a biased-noise colour code with domain walls plus a restriction decoder), while P is a NISQ variational circuit-compression method for nonadiabatic chemistry dynamics; nothing in P encodes qubits or produces syndromes, so there is no concrete hook beyond the generic 'noisy hardware would benefit from error correction'. The only stress-style link is that P's compression is tuned to hardware fidelity and dominant noise, which could in principle be biased, but Q offers no logical-gate or resource-estimate machinery that P's Trotter/compressed circuits could actually consume. The integration story is the universal-adapter kind — any error-correcting code attaches to any algorithmic demo — so interest stays low.

Q is a multi-client blind delegation protocol built on a photonic linear network (Qline) with single-qubit state relaying, whereas P is a silicon exchange-only QPU with cryo-CMOS control demonstrating a distance-5 repetition code; the only concrete hook is the generic 'untrusted remote server' framing, since Q's measurement-based, photonic Qline construction cannot be implemented on P's spin-qubit chip without a wholly different architecture and no interconnect or photonic interface is described. Blind delegation is the universal-adapter pattern here — it attaches to any cloud-accessible QPU paper equally well, and nothing about exchange-only qubits, the ribbon cable, or the repetition-code demo is specifically stressed or served by multi-client blindness. A curator could sketch a 'privacy for silicon cloud QPUs' note, but it would be generic and would not change how either paper is read.

Both papers concern error mitigation applied to a quantum characterisation or learning task, but on incompatible platforms: Q's recycling mitigation is specific to photon loss in linear optics, whereas P's noise scaling exploits an involutory fan-out coupling on superconducting qubits, so neither technique transfers to the other's hardware. The nearest hook is generic — P's direct tomography could in principle certify the output distribution of a Born machine — but a QCBM's output is a sampled classical distribution rather than a sparse density matrix, and P's constant-depth meter-qubit gadget has no linear-optical analogue. That leaves a universal-adapter style pairing (any state-verification scheme against any generative model demo) with no experiment either group could actually run on shared hardware.

Q is a symbolic-execution verifier for the fault-tolerance of QECC gadget implementations, whereas P is a QM/QM/MM multiscale embedding platform for covalent drug docking whose quantum content is 20-qubit NISQ chemistry runs plus fault-tolerant resource estimates; there is no concrete hook, since P specifies no QECC implementation or logical gadget for Q to verify, and P's resource counts are logical-level estimates rather than circuits with error combinations to enumerate. The only bridge is the shared aspiration to future fault-tolerant hardware, which is an area overlap rather than a technique that transfers or composes. Any integration story would be of the universal-adapter kind, applying equally to every chemistry paper mentioning fault tolerance, so interest is low."}

Q is a QAOA heuristic for approximate CVP in lattice cryptanalysis, analysed largely numerically with fixed pre-trained angles, while P is a hardware tomography protocol using fan-out couplings to a meter qubit for sparse-state and GHZ verification; there is no shared technique, no claim of Q's that P stresses, and no circuit-level hook beyond both being quantum. Both axes therefore sit near zero.

Both papers sit in the QML-on-real-hardware family, but the only shared content is the generic task framing (binary classification with a quantum feature extractor plus classical post-processing); the platforms are incompatible in kind, since Q's contribution is adaptive state injection into particle-number-preserving linear optical interferometers, which has no counterpart in Aquila's analogue Rydberg evolution, and P's Quantum Evolution Kernel needs a graph-to-register embedding that a Boson Sampling convolutional layer does not provide. Interest is correspondingly low because the pairing would generate a generic 'compare two QML kernels' dossier that attaches to any photonic-versus-neutral-atom classifier pair.

Q is an abstract categorical result showing that mixed quantum dynamics and classical reversible computation both arise from a universal restriction-affine completion, with no circuit-level, hardware, or estimation content; P is an experimental NMR/OTOC protocol using AlphaEvolve-optimised fSim circuits and Pauli-path zero-noise extrapolation on Willow. The only shared notion is that Stinespring dilation underlies open-system channels generally, which is background theory rather than a hook P uses, needs, or can compose with. Both papers use fixed parameterized circuits, but QuIC is explicitly training-free with fixed angles chosen for injectivity of the sorted output distribution, so Q's contribution — a perturbative update rule replacing variational optimisation of parameters — has nothing to optimise in P's pipeline, and P's graph-isomorphism separation claim is not stressed by Q's energy-minimisation results. The only hook is the shared MaxCut/graph substrate: one could imagine using Q's discrete adiabatic scheme on graph problems, but that is a different task from embedding rather than a modification of P's circuit. Interest is low because the pairing is generic parameterized-circuit family membership, and any concrete experiment would abandon precisely the training-free property that defines P.

Q is a variational/adiabatic ground-state optimisation method built on parameterised circuits and classical linear-system updates, whereas P realises open-system quantum trajectories with mid-circuit measurement and feedback to reach a non-equilibrium steady state — a driven-dissipative dynamics problem with no ground-state variational objective for Q's perturbative parameter-update equations to act on. The only hook is the shared Ising/hard-core-boson lattice Hamiltonian family (Q tests the transverse-field Ising chain), which is a topical rather than technical overlap: Q's discrete adiabatic sweep neither prepares P's steady state nor stresses its claims, and P's mid-circuit measurement capability is irrelevant to Q's observable-measurement scheme. A curator could at best imagine variationally preparing initial states for the trajectory circuits, a generic and weakly motivated story given the steady state is independent of initialisation.

Q modifies Clifford randomized benchmarking by replacing the inverse operator with a stabiliser-verification acceptance test and extends interleaved RB to non-Clifford gates via gate synthesis, all in the single-circuit, low-error characterisation setting; P is an empirical study of inter-circuit crosstalk between concurrently scheduled tenants on IBM Heron/Nighthawk devices, quantified by SSIM and t-statistics over output distributions of QAOA, Grover, QPE, QFT and ZZFeatureMap. The only hook is generic — one could in principle run Q's verification-based RB as a co-tenant probe to give a scalar figure of merit for interference instead of P's SSIM comparisons — but nothing in Q addresses spatially correlated, cross-register crosstalk, which RB's twirling assumptions actively wash out, so the two techniques neither transfer nor compose concretely. The proposal is of the universal-adapter kind, since any benchmarking protocol could be dropped into a multitenant scheduler study, and neither the acceptance-probability figure of merit nor the non-Clifford synthesis machinery is specific to P's circuit-affinity claims.

Both sit squarely in QEC decoding/hardware demonstration, and there is a concrete hook: P explicitly names exponential classical post-processing in code distance as one of the two main barriers to scaling error detection, and runs repetition and triangular colour codes on up to 74 qubits, while Q supplies a parallelisable reliability-guided inversion decoder for arbitrary QLDPC codes (colour codes included) with reduced sub-threshold runtime and hardware-implementable structure, so P's post-selection/decoding pipeline could be re-run with LSD to test whether the classical bottleneck actually binds. Interest is above generic because the constraint is shared and specific — real-time syndrome processing on as-built devices — but it is tempered by the fact that P's regime is error detection with post-selection on small distances, where Q's asymptotic sub-threshold complexity gains are least pronounced, and by LSD being a general-purpose decoder that attaches to most QLDPC hardware papers.

Q is a compendium of metrics and benchmarking methodologies for quantum computers, while P is a domain-specific simulation of large-N QCD2 kink-antikink potentials on IBM Nighthawk; the only hook is that P's hardware run is benchmarked against exact diagonalisation and MPS references, which Q's application-level benchmarking taxonomy and reproducibility criteria could formalise, and Q's call for reporting standards could be applied to P's postselection and error-cancellation claims. That is a generic auditing overlay rather than a technique that composes with P's disorder-operator circuit or stresses its physics claims, so correctness sits at the level of same-area-with-weak-hook. Interest is low because a benchmark-and-reporting compendium attaches to essentially any hardware demonstration paper, the universal-adapter pattern, with nothing specific to bosonised QCD2 or the XXZ mapping.

Q gives an optimised adiabatic schedule for Grover-type unstructured search with parallelisation and bounded-coherence protocols, while P (judged from title alone) is a Gaussian-boson-sampling-style photonic sampling advantage demonstration; a non-universal photonic sampler cannot run an adiabatic oracle-based search, so no concrete technical hook transfers or composes. The only shared ground is the generic notion of quantum advantage under limited resources, which is topical rather than technical, and P's sampling claim is not stressed by a search-speedup bound. A curator would find no specific integration story beyond the universal 'advantage under constraints' framing.

Both papers concern non-independent, correlated noise in real devices, and P's demonstration that environment-mediated correlations qualitatively alter outcomes on IBM hardware speaks directly to the assumption Q rejects, but the hook stays conceptual: P studies a two-qubit Deutsch circuit with no encoding, so Q's Clifford-conjugated surface code and matching decoder have no workload in P to attach to, and P supplies no per-qubit noise-bias characterisation of the kind Q's tailoring consumes. At best P offers qualitative evidence that correlated dephasing exists, which Q already asserts, so neither stresses nor composes with the other concretely. Interest is limited because the pairing reduces to the generic observation that codes should be tailored to correlated noise, an argument attachable to any correlated-noise characterisation paper.

Both papers converge on a concrete hook: Q's randomised compilation twirls arbitrary logical circuit noise into stochastic Pauli form and certifies encoded runs device-independently, while P learns a full Kraus/crosstalk/SPAM model on ibm_fez and explicitly uses it to assess QAOA with an error-detection scheme — precisely the encoded regime where P's fitted model is an unvalidated extrapolation that Q's accreditation could bound, and conversely P's learned noise model supplies the general (coherent, crosstalk-correlated) noise against which Q's robustness claims and crossover predictions could be simulated before hardware time is spent. The pairing is more than the universal-adapter pattern because P's error-detected QAOA prediction is exactly the quantity Q's framework certifies and because P's non-Pauli crosstalk channels are the assumption Q's twirl is designed to remove, so int is high but not maximal: noise-model fitting remains a broadly attachable technique and the composition would need P to move beyond its current physical-level circuits.

Q is a resource-estimation and circuit-construction paper for a Grover oracle solving SVP, with costs quoted in qubits, T-count and depth for fault-tolerant scales; P is a near-term error-mitigation study fitting physically bounded ZNE models to shallow GHZ/W circuits. There is no concrete hook: Q's oracle produces a single marked-state search outcome rather than the expectation values ZNE corrects, and its circuit sizes are far beyond the noisy devices P benchmarks, so the techniques neither transfer nor compose. Any pairing would rest on the universal-adapter claim that ZNE attaches to any quantum circuit, which is generic and specific to neither side.

Q delivers verifiable blind quantum computing over a trapped-ion server with photonic client detection, whereas P is a perspective on variational algorithms for CFD illustrated on 1D Burgers' equation; there is no shared technique, and the only hook is the generic observation that a variational CFD workload run on a cloud QPU could in principle be delegated blindly. That hook is weak on both sides: Q's measurement-based interactive protocol targets small verified computations, not the hundreds of qubits and deep variational optimisation loops P envisages, and P raises no confidentiality requirement (no proprietary geometry or data privacy threat model) that would make blindness the missing ingredient. The privacy-wrapper story attaches equally to any NISQ application paper, which is the universal-adapter pattern and caps interest well below the threshold.

Q builds a shot-budget- and error-mitigation-aware benchmarking framework whose figure of merit is confidence that an estimated energy falls between classical bounds for a combinatorial/Fermi-Hubbard optimisation problem, whereas P reports a hybrid ResNet-50 plus variational circuit classifier for blood cell images; there is no energy estimate, no classical bound interval, and no PEC-style sampling overhead in P's pipeline, so Q's machinery does not transfer.
